newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Last Post for 1,000-day British regiment in H.K.
newsitem.headline: Last Post for 1,000-day British regiment in H.K.

text.p: To the haunting notes of the Last Post from a lone buglar, Britain closed another chapter in the colonial history book on Saturday by disbanding its shortest-lived peacetime regiment.
Dubbed the 1,000 Day Regiment, the Hong Kong Logistic Support Regiment's job is done just one month and a day before the British flag is furled over its last Asian outpost.
The last British soldier will march out of Hong Kong shortly after the stroke of midnight on June 30, marking the end of more than 150 years of colonial rule.

"It is not often that one bears witness not only to the formation but also the disbandment of a regiment," the commander of British Forces, Major General Bryan Dutton, told the troops parading in the the unrelenting glare of the tropical sun.
"It was formed as a regiment which would have a life of 1,000 days. It has actually lasted a little longer -- 1,181 days," he said.

In its short lifetime, the Logistic Support Regiment -- motto: "We sustain" -- has sold off the fleet of Royal Air Force Wessex helicopters to Uruguay and the Royal Navy's three Peacock class patrol boats to the Philippines.
Its troops presided over one of the most ambitious garage sales in Hong Kong.
Everything had to go. From boots to bedroom suites, cars to mess crockery, food, ammunition and sporting equipment.
They mothballed Stanley Fort which housed the resident infantry battalion and decommissioned military schools.
Yet they continued to supply to what remained of the British garrison what Commanding Officer Lt Colonel Nigel Lloyd called essential services -- "everything from broomsticks to bayonets".
Only about 1,000 British military and civilian personnel remain in the British garrison in Hong Kong, the second oldest after Gibraltar, down from more than 10,000 during its peacetime heyday.
"I am naturally emotionally upset that it is time to go," said Lloyd as the regiment prepared to vacate the last barracks occupied by British troops on the Chinese mainland.
Osborn Barracks, situated in a leafy suburb on the Kowloon peninsula directly below the flight path of the airport, will be handed over to the Hong Kong government next week.
The government in turn will pass the barracks and other former British military facilities, including some of the world's most valuable real estate, on to the incoming Chinese garrison.

A third group of 90 Chinese troops drove across the border on Friday to join 106 colleagues already stationed in Hong Kong. They will prepare for the arrival of the full Chinese garrison expected to number about 10,000 troops at its peak.
After the pipes and drums of the Black Watch, the last resident British regiment to be stationed in Hong Kong, struck up the farewell song Auld Lang Syne, Dutton summed up his feelings.
"It's a combination of sadness that something which is intrinsically good... has to come to an end and those relationships break up," the 61st and last commander of British Forces in Asia said.
"And on the other hand there is a sense of pride because they have done an amazing job," he said as the 1,000 Day Regiment marched briskly into history.
